idiom_name: sender-stamped expiration plus broker/consumer enforcement with dead-lettering
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the sender attaches an expiration to the message (an absolute UTC deadline where possible, a TTL only if a single hop will convert it), then two enforcement points are configured. The messaging system enforces at entity or message level - discarding or routing expired messages to a dead-letter path with a distinguishable reason - and the receiver re-checks the same deadline on arrival and again before side effects, discarding anything stale instead of processing it. Monotonic clocks are used for local timing decisions and an absolute UTC timestamp for the wire; every converting hop accepts and records a bounded skew. Expiry without a dead-letter channel, metric or alert is indistinguishable from data loss, so the pattern is only complete when discarded messages are observable.
code_sketch:
send(msg, ttl = 60s)                     # broker stamps expires_at = now + ttl

consume(msg):
    if msg.expires_at <= now_utc():      # first line of defence: re-check
        dead_letter(msg, reason="expired")
        return
    process(msg)                         # only work whose result still matters
pitfalls: Using a process-local monotonic deadline as the value on the wire; peers cannot compare it, so the message either never expires or expires immediately.
Enforcing expiry only in the broker: a message already delivered or locked for delivery can still be stale when it is finally processed.
Discarding expired messages without a dead-letter path, reason code or metric, so lateness becomes invisible data loss.

Wrong move: Treat subscription retention as a per-message freshness deadline -> replay and storage semantics do not prevent a consumer from applying an old message -> instead carry an explicit deadline and re-check it before side effects.

Wrong move: Assume a broker TTL frees resources immediately when any message expires -> lazy head-of-queue expiry can leave stale payloads occupying memory -> instead monitor backlog and use queue-level controls or an expiry-aware queue when prompt reclamation is required.

Wrong move: Shorten TTL under load as a substitute for backpressure -> overload is converted into silent business loss while service health looks falsely green -> instead apply bounded queues or backpressure, scale consumers, and alert on expired or dead-lettered messages.
